name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
title: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
answer: Keeping financial data out of public models means preventing account balances, transaction records, payroll details, trading positions, client identities, material nonpublic information, internal forecasts, and any prompt that contains them from reaching hosted model services that may log, retain, or train on inputs. The scope covers direct use of public chatbots, embedded AI features in accounting and customer relationship software, fine-tuning jobs, embedding pipelines, and third-party tools that finance staff adopt without review. It also covers the data that surrounds a model, such as evaluation sets, support tickets, and telemetry that can carry sensitive values. The aim is not to ban AI in finance but to keep confidential financial data inside approved boundaries while still allowing routine work.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Controls for this work run on data classification and tagging, tokenization, redaction, and format preserving encryption before any prompt leaves a controlled environment. Private model endpoints, dedicated cloud tenancies, virtual private clouds, on premises inference servers, and API gateways with allow lists keep traffic away from public consumer endpoints. Identity and access management, secrets management, key management, data loss prevention, egress filtering, and audit logging provide the surrounding enforcement. Retrieval systems add permission aware indexes and vector stores so that a model can only see documents the requesting user is already entitled to see. Monitoring tools watch for unusual prompt patterns, bulk exports, and attempts to reconstruct training data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The daily work starts with data discovery and classification, then maps where financial data enters prompts, plugins, connectors, and model training sets. Teams minimize data before use, replace identifiers with tokens or synthetic values, and route requests through gateways that strip or block sensitive fields. They test controls with red team exercises, prompt injection attempts, canary records, and model inversion probes, then review logs and alerts. Vendor due diligence covers retention settings, training use, subprocessors, breach notice terms, and deletion rights, with results recorded in a model or system inventory. Where a use case cannot be made safe, the practice is to redesign the workflow, use a private model, or decline the use case rather than rely on a single filter.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here come from confidentiality duties, fiduciary obligations, insider trading rules, privacy law, sector rules for financial records, cross border transfer limits, and contractual terms with clients and vendors. Provenance matters because a firm may need to show what data trained or prompted a model, which version was used, who approved it, and how long inputs were retained. The atlas tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages and 147 active AI lawsuits, which reflects how much enforcement and litigation surrounds data handling and AI use. Common risks include memorization of rare values, reidentification from supposedly anonymous data, vendor secondary use, privilege waiver, and discovery exposure. Governance usually combines policy, training, approval gates, audit trails, and clear ownership for financial data that touches any model.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward smaller private models, on device inference, confidential computing, and data clean rooms that let analysis happen without raw financial records leaving a controlled boundary. Synthetic data, differential privacy, and federated learning are being tested to reduce the need to expose real values to any model. Policy enforcement is moving into gateways and data platforms, so classification and redaction happen automatically rather than through manual review. Regulators and auditors are asking for model inventories, provenance records, and evidence that retention and deletion promises are real. The likely result is not a single block on public models but a tiered approach, where low risk tasks use public tools under strict controls and high risk financial data stays in private or isolated environments.
